facts.claim: All tracks on American Football (LP3) are credited as written by American Football, and Hayley Williams is credited with additional vocals on 'Uncomfortably Numb'.

Jason Cupp is credited as engineer, mixer and producer on LP3. The credits also list Mike Kinsella, Steve Holmes and Nate Kinsella as group members, and Hayley Williams as featured artist and vocalist.
The band used the same producer (Jason Cupp) and the same studio (Arc Studios in Omaha, Nebraska) as on LP2, but took a markedly different approach to the recording.
Kristina Dutton played violin and wrote the violin arrangements on 'Uncomfortably Numb', 'Silhouettes' and 'Life Support'.

The song was released as a single on January 22, 2019, with a music video. Rolling Stone described it as earnest but more pop-leaning than the band's earlier music, with Kinsella and Williams singing about youthful regrets and more naive relationships.

The video was directed by Atiba Jefferson. It is mostly a point-of-view depiction of the aftermath of an emergency incident, with the victim treated by paramedics. It followed the single 'Silhouettes' from December 2018.
The video has cameos from Blake Anderson of Workaholics, pro skater Paul Rodriguez and Samhain drummer London May.
Describing LP3 in a press release, Kinsella said LP2 was about working out how to use the band's different 'arms'. For LP3 the band decided to use them.

LP3 was the first American Football album with outside guest vocalists singing alongside Mike Kinsella. They were Hayley Williams on 'Uncomfortably Numb', Elizabeth Powell of Land of Talk and Rachel Goswell of Slowdive. AllMusic said Williams' powerful style risks overpowering Kinsella and adds a pop sheen at odds with the resigned lyrics.

American Football formed in 1997 in Urbana, Illinois, when Mike Kinsella, Steve Lamos and Steve Holmes were students at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Kinsella's nephew Nate Kinsella joined for the reunion shows.

research.lineage: The song sits in the emo and Midwest emo tradition, with chiming, twinkly guitars from the Kinsella family's Illinois scene, and it pushes toward a more polished, pop-leaning sound through the Paramore guest vocal.

draft:
The line that gives **Uncomfortably Numb** away is a confession built like a punchline: "Now, as a father, I blame the booze." Just before it, the narrator admits to blaming their own father as a kid. The symmetry is the wound. Blame hasn't gone anywhere. It has moved down a generation and picked a new target. The narrator sees the pattern clearly and still can't climb out of it, and that clarity is what makes the numbness uncomfortable rather than restful. The title takes a familiar phrase and makes it itch.

The song keeps stacking that kind of honesty next to self-protection. "All my sympathy prescribed" turns feeling into something dosed out. "Struggling for two" turns parenthood into a heavier load rather than a cure. Then a verse begins tenderly and slides into an admission of having pushed someone around to break them in. It's never clear whether the "you" is a partner or the drink itself. The verse ends in surrender either way, then snaps back to the family line: "Comatose, like father like son." Through all of it, questions in parentheses cut in, asking whose ugly side is ugliest, like a second conscience talking over the first.

Mike Kinsella and Hayley Williams of Paramore share the song. It's the first time American Football brought outside voices onto a record, a band whose roots go back to a 1997 dorm-room start in Urbana, Illinois. The music still runs on the chiming, interlocking guitar logic of that Midwest emo scene. Clean electric arpeggios sit over a walking bass line, and the drums keep a steady, driving pulse with the snare out front, all at an unhurried middle tempo. The lead vocal is clear and slightly breathy, holding notes instead of pushing them. Jason Cupp produced again at Arc Studios in Omaha, and the sound is polished and roomy. Kristina Dutton wrote and played the violin parts. Kinsella has said that the band spent its previous album figuring out how to use its different arms, and this time it decided to use them.

Some critics found Williams' power a little much, a pop sheen laid over lyrics that sound resigned. That friction is real, but it may be the point. A bright, steady band carries someone describing going under, which is how numbness tends to look from outside. The last verse goes darker and funnier at once: "I'll make new friends in the ambulance." The video, directed by Atiba Jefferson, takes that line at its word, a point-of-view ride through an emergency and its aftermath.

The song sticks because it describes the feeling of not feeling so precisely that you end up carrying the ache the narrator says is gone.

factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly.

factCheck.note: Lyric: "I blamed my father in my youth."

factCheck.claim: Quotes of "All my sympathy prescribed" and "Struggling for two"
factCheck.note: The wording is accurate, but five quoted lyric lines exceeds the three-line limit. Both are now paraphrased without quote marks.

factCheck.claim: Verse begins gentle and slides into having pushed someone around to break them in; the verse ends with "I've tried but you've won"
factCheck.note: Matches "We were gentle to begin / Then I pushed you around to break you in" and "I've tried but you've won." The partner-or-drink reading is interpretation.

factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly.

factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly.
